analysis.one_liner: Opens more federal offshore waters and public lands to oil and gas drilling and shifts permitting power to states.
analysis.headline: The House Natural Resources Committee approved the bill 19–14 and sent it to the House calendar, but it never got a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have opened more of the outer Continental Shelf and federal lands to oil and gas drilling. It would have shared federal drilling revenues with a handful of coastal states, stripped the President's power to block drilling in offshore waters, thrown out an Arctic drilling safety rule, let states take over federal drilling permits and fracking rules, and made it faster and easier for companies to get permits that affect marine mammals. It also required offshore wind lease sales off California and Hawaii.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies gain the most: more offshore areas available for leasing, mandatory execution of scheduled lease sales, no presidential authority to withdraw waters from drilling, elimination of the 2016 Arctic exploratory drilling safety rule, state-run permitting on federal land with federal fracking rules preempted, and faster marine mammal permits with provisions deemed approved if the government misses deadlines. Coastal and producing states gain a share of federal drilling revenue (up to 50% under later phases) and direct royalty payments. Offshore wind developers gain mandated lease sales off California, Hawaii, and several territories.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies; coastal state governments

how_it_helps.text: Shares federal offshore oil and gas revenue with Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alaska, and increases the capped share going to Gulf producing states for fiscal years 2029–2059.

Removes the President's general authority to withdraw outer Continental Shelf waters from oil and gas leasing, voids most existing withdrawals, and bars the President from creating new marine national monuments.
Requires Interior to execute every unexecuted lease sale from the most recent leasing program and lets the Secretary deem environmental review satisfied at its own discretion.
Nullifies the 2016 federal rule setting safety requirements for exploratory drilling in the Arctic outer Continental Shelf.

Lets qualifying states take over issuing federal drilling permits and approving drilling plans, provides states a property interest in their royalty share paid directly by operators, and bars Interior from enforcing any federal hydraulic fracturing rule in states that have their own rules.

Sets hard deadlines for marine mammal incidental-take permits—deemed issued after 120 days without a decision—and exempts those takings from Endangered Species Act consultation, while establishing user fees to fund offshore and onshore safety inspections.
Requires a wind lease sale off the coast of California within a year of enactment and wind lease sales off Hawaii and several U.S. territories if found feasible.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers lose revenue that would otherwise go to the Treasury, since up to half of offshore leasing revenue is redirected to a few states and to designated funds. Coastal communities face increased exposure to offshore drilling and spill risk where protections are stripped, and the public bears the cost of weakened federal oversight: state-run permitting on federal land, state fracking rules replacing federal ones, an Arctic safety rule erased, and marine mammal protections that default to approval when deadlines lapse.

drawbacks.text: Stripping the President's power to withdraw offshore waters from drilling, and voiding most existing withdrawals, removes the main check that has kept large parts of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Alaskan outer Continental Shelf unleased.

Nullifying the 2016 Arctic exploratory drilling rule eliminates safety requirements written after years of experience with harsh, remote Arctic conditions, where a spill would be exceptionally difficult to contain.

Preempting all federal hydraulic fracturing rules wherever a state has any rules of its own means drilling on federal land would be held to widely varying state standards rather than a national floor.

Deeming marine mammal take permits approved after 120 days of inaction, limiting permit conditions to changes that do not alter a project's design, and exempting those takings from Endangered Species Act consultation reduces review of harm to whales and other protected species.

Redirecting up to half of offshore drilling revenue to a handful of states reduces federal receipts that currently serve all taxpayers, and creates a fiscal incentive for states to back more drilling off their coasts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a genuine package, not one-sided: it funds safety inspections through new fees, adds offshore wind lease sales, and gives coastal states a share of drilling revenue. But its center of gravity is expanding oil and gas access while trimming federal oversight—erasing an Arctic safety rule, preempting federal fracking standards, and weakening marine mammal review. The revenue sharing would partly compensate the states closest to drilling, but the broader environmental and fiscal costs would fall on the public as a whole. On balance, the costs outweigh the modest benefits for anyone not in the drilling industry.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved and reported it with an amendment in November 2018, but it sat on the House calendar and never came up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on November 3, 2017 and referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
The committee held markups on November 7–8, 2017 and ordered the bill reported amended by a 19–14 vote.
The committee formally reported the bill with an amendment on November 2, 2018 (H. Rept. 115-1000), one day before the 2018 election, and it was placed on the Union Calendar.
The bill never received a vote in the full House or any action in the Senate before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coastal communities and the offshore waters the bill would have opened are better off that it died: no new Atlantic or Alaskan leasing mandate, the Arctic drilling safety rule stayed in effect, and federal fracking and marine mammal protections remained intact. The oil and gas industry did not gain the expanded access and streamlined permitting the bill offered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coastal communities; drilling protections stayed intact

sides.party_line_note: The committee report vote of 19–14 split along party lines, and 14 of the 16 cosponsors were Republicans; the two Democratic cosponsors were both from Texas oil country.

industries.note: The bill expands access to offshore and federal lands, mandates lease sales, voids the Arctic drilling safety rule, preempts federal fracking standards, and speeds marine mammal permits—all of which lower costs and barriers for drillers while shifting spill and oversight risk to the public and coastal communities.
The bill requires a wind lease sale off California within a year and conditional sales off Hawaii and several territories, creating new commercial opportunities for renewable energy developers.

Producing and nearby coastal states would receive up to 50% of offshore leasing revenue plus direct royalty payments, but the money only flows if drilling happens off their coasts, which exposes their residents and tourism and fishing economies to spill risk.

By mandating lease sales and limiting presidential withdrawals, the bill expands drilling in waters used by fishing and tourism businesses that bear the downside of any spill or disruption; these industries' interest runs with the public's in keeping waters unleased.
